transcript.text: Worcester Greenstar 30i combi - pressure keeps dropping to about 0.5 bar every few days and I have to top it up. Can you help me work out why?

A Worcester Bosch Greenstar 30i losing pressure repeatedly (dropping from ~1.5 bar to 0.5 bar every few days) is not normal. While a very small amount of air loss over months can happen, daily or weekly drops indicate an issue that needs addressing.

Here’s a step-by-step guide to help you diagnose the problem:

### ⚠️ Important Safety Note
• Never open the sealed combustion chamber of your boiler.
• If you smell gas at any point, turn off the gas supply immediately and call the Gas Safe Register emergency line (0800 111 999 in the UK).
• If you are unsure about any step, contact a Gas Safe registered engineer.

---

## 🔍 Most Common Causes & How to Check Them

### 1. Leak in the Central Heating System (Most Likely)
This is the #1 cause of repeated pressure loss. Water escapes somewhere in your radiators, pipes, or underfloor heating.

How to check:
• Visual inspection: Look around all radiators (especially at the valves and top/bottom corners), pipe joints, and under sinks/boiler area for dampness, corrosion, or white/green scale deposits.
• Check the pressure relief valve (PRV): Located on the boiler’s cold water inlet. If it’s dripping or has discharged recently, it could be leaking internally or externally.
• Monitor overnight: Turn off the heating system completely, note the pressure, and check again in the morning. If it dropped significantly while the system was cold and unused, you likely have a leak.

### 2. Faulty Pressure Relief Valve (PRV)
The PRV releases water if pressure gets too high. If it’s faulty, it may drip slowly even when pressure is normal.

How to check:
• Look under the boiler for any signs of recent dripping or corrosion around the PRV discharge pipe (usually a copper tube going outside).
• If you see water coming from this pipe when the system cools down after heating, the PRV may be sticking open.

### 3. Faulty Expansion Vessel
The expansion vessel absorbs excess pressure as water heats up. If its internal rubber bladder has failed or lost its air charge, it can cause pressure fluctuations and leaks via the PRV.

How to check (requires some technical knowledge):
• Turn off the boiler and let the system cool completely.
• Isolate the boiler from the heating system (close isolation valves if you know how).
• Use a bicycle pump or pressure gauge on the Schrader valve (like a tire valve) on the expansion vessel. If it releases water, the bladder is burst. If there’s no air pressure when the system is empty, the vessel needs recharging or replacing.
• Note: This often requires an engineer if you’re not comfortable.

### 4. Leaking Automatic Air Vent (AAV)
Air vents on radiators or manifolds can leak water if the seal fails.

How to check:
• Inspect all air vents in your system for dampness or corrosion around the vent head.
• Try closing the vent slightly (use a flathead screwdriver) and see if pressure stabilizes. Don’t over-tighten.

### 5. Faulty Fill Loop / External Leak
If you��ve been topping up frequently, check your fill loop (the flexible hose used to repressurize). It may not be fully closed or could have a slow leak at the connections.

---

## ✅ What You Should Do Next

1. Check for visible leaks: Inspect all radiators, pipes, and under the boiler.
2. Monitor pressure overnight: Turn off heating, note pressure, check next morning.
3. Inspect the PRV discharge pipe for drips.
4. If no obvious leak is found, the issue is likely internal (expansion vessel or hidden leak).

## 🛠️ When to Call a Gas Safe Engineer
You should call a professional if:
• You can’t find a visible leak but pressure keeps dropping.
• The expansion vessel needs testing/recharging.
• There’s water around the PRV or boiler casing.
• You’re uncomfortable performing any of these checks.

A Gas Safe engineer can:
• Pressure test the system to isolate leaks.
• Test and recharge/replace the expansion vessel.
• Check the PRV and safety valves.
• Fix any hidden leaks in pipework or radiators.

## 💡 Temporary Measure (Not a Solution)
You can use a leak detection dye (available at DIY stores) added to your heating system to help pinpoint small leaks, but this doesn’t fix the root cause.

Let me know if you’d like more detailed instructions on any of these steps!

I've checked and there's nothing obvious under the boiler or around the radiators and pipes, and the carpets are dry. The little copper pipe outside the wall does drip sometimes, more when the heating's on. No gas smell, and my CO alarm isn't going off. I haven't got the tools or training to work on the boiler itself, so is this something I can fix myself or does it need an engineer?

Based on your description—specifically that the copper pipe outside drips more when the heating is on—this strongly points to a faulty expansion vessel or a failed internal seal within the boiler.

Here’s what you need to know:

### 🛠️ Can You Fix This Yourself?
No. This requires a Gas Safe registered engineer for several reasons:
1.  Safety & Legal: The expansion vessel is part of the sealed heating system. Accessing it involves draining parts of the central heating and potentially opening boiler casings, which is illegal for anyone who isn’t Gas Safe certified in the UK.
2.  Complexity: Even if you could access it, diagnosing whether it’s just a lost air pressure in the vessel (which can sometimes be topped up) or a completely failed bladder requires specific tools and knowledge. If the bladder has ruptured, water gets into the air side of the vessel, which is not user-repairable.
3.  Risk: Attempting to open the boiler casing yourself will void your warranty and could create safety hazards (gas leaks, electrical issues).

### 🔍 What’s Likely Happening?
When you heat the water in your system, it expands. Normally, this extra pressure is absorbed by the expansion vessel. If the vessel’s internal rubber bladder has failed:
• The expanded water has nowhere to go but out through the Pressure Relief Valve (PRV).
• This causes the drip you see on the copper pipe outside.
• Because water is escaping, your system pressure drops.
• You top up the pressure, but the next time you heat the system, it expands again and leaks more water out of the PRV.

### ✅ What Should You Do?
1.  Call a Gas Safe Registered Engineer. Explain that:
• Pressure drops repeatedly.
• The external discharge pipe (PRV) is dripping when the heating is on.
• No visible leaks are found in radiators or pipes.
2.  Ask them to check the expansion vessel first. This is a common and often less expensive repair than replacing the whole boiler. They will:
• Check the air pressure in the vessel with a tyre gauge (while the system is cold and depressurised).
• Determine if the bladder needs re-pressurising or if the vessel itself needs replacement.

### 💡 Temporary Measure
Until you get an engineer, top up the pressure only when it drops below 0.5 bar to prevent the boiler from locking out. Avoid topping it up excessively (e.g., above 1.8–2.0 bar) as this may cause more frequent dripping from the external pipe.

This is a very common issue with Greenstar boilers, and a qualified engineer should be able to diagnose and fix it efficiently.
